review: buy this fantastic game before they delist it for a more expensive version

I've seen a lot of reviews try to win people over with an endless list of amusing anecdotes - winning chickens in a bowling game and making them a real estate manager. Training a dominatrix to be more assertive. Obliterating people in combat with a motorcycle.

It's all true, of course. Yakuza 0 can be an immensely funny and absurd game with moments that's genuinely make you laugh out loud - largely because you could have never expected them.

But I also think that's had the side effect of selling the game short. You might think this is a comedy game, something that is almost lighthearted or trivial.

It's not.

Yakuza 0 is a very serious game - a fact you might find surprising. Its plot is complex and is centered on a fairly dry subject of real estate intrigue in a booming market. It deals with mature, often terrible issues and has a cast of immensely realistic - and likable - characters set in an equally realistic city. Yakuza has the pacing and tone of a drama, and it must be enjoyed slowly like one.

The comedy, then, is not the driver of this game, but rather serves as a much needed relief of tension. It's almost like there's a swinging pendulum in which the game is allowed to present you with increasingly intense and dramatic moments so long as it's all offset by an equally increasing level of absurdity. It helps space out the moments of self-seriousness in a way that just...works.

Beyond just the tone and story is a very enjoyable brawler that constantly mixes it up with minigames, tough bosses, and other diversions. I do want to stress that this isn't necessarily a game you're coming back to for the gameplay - rather, you'll be coming for the story, the characters, the city itself.

This isn't a bad thing, though, and I wish more games would take this approach. Yakuza 0 is a wonderful game.

PS: Whoever did the localization for Yakuza 0 is a fucking genius.

You either give up within first few hours of Yakuza 0 or you enjoy every single second of it and buy all Yakuza games on Steam. There's no in-between.

[h1]Yakuza 0 is the best Real-Estate Management and Cabaret Club simulator with a Yakuza action adventure minigame ever made.[/h1]

[b] Yakuza 0 is an unapologetically explosive, bombastic, and absolutely fabulous adventure in the shining lights of 80’s Japan and with the sheer amount of content in this game per the price itself, it is a must for fans of open world games. [/b]

[h1][b]+Pros[/b][/h1]

[h1][b]+Story[/b][/h1]
Yakuza 0 follows the origin stories of two series regulars Kazuma Kiryu and Goro Majima. It explains their starting relationships with several other characters who appear in future Yakuza games as well as showing their individual growth to becoming the legendary characters long time fans are more familiar with. Basically, if you're intimidated to dive in because it may be difficult to understand the story don't be, the in game story is just beginning so it's relatively easy to understand for newcomers. 


As for the stories themselves, although they play out mostly like a dramatic Japanese soap-opera with lots of yelling and intense zoom ins, they are actually quite interesting with many twists and turns, betrayal, and even a tragic romance which leads to a very interesting and compelling narrative that also isn’t afraid to amp up the machismo factor whenever you’re having a shirts off, hand to hand brawl with one of the big Yakuza bosses. 

[h1] [b]+Combat[/b] [/h1]
For those of you more familiar with the Batman: Arkham series with the punch a lot of enemies and then press a button to counter when you’re about to get hit combat system here you’ll find the combat in Yakuza 0 to be completely different despite them both being 3rd person action fighting games.

For example, Yakuza 0’s combat system is a lot more interactive with both Kiryu and Majima containing several distinct fighting styles to defeat a lot of enemies in a truly satisfying manner.

Whether it be Kiryu’s straightforward pummeling to beat a group of enemies or Majima’s fabulous breakdancing you’ll find the fighting in this game to always be fun as hell and satisfying once you get used to the rhythm.

My favorite part of the combat system however is definitely the mechanic of “heat actions” where once you build up enough heat meter, you can do some wild actions to deal tons of damage to whoever so happens to be unlucky enough to be in your way.

Here’s some examples.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hgozp1pyaBc

Oh and there’s no counter button to instantly respond when attacked unless you either count Kiryu’s Brawler style to punch back instantly after getting hit or later on with another style you unlock so if you get jumped from behind and get comboed by multiple people expect to actually take some damage. 

It shouldn’t be too much of an issue however as later on you’ll be able to easily solo twenty enemies or more once you unlock all the styles.

[h1][b]+Soundtrack[/b][/h1]
Yakuza 0 has an amazing soundtrack to really get into the groove when you’re pummeling hordes of enemies, fighting an epic boss battle, or just tryin to groove at the karaoke bar Yakuza 0 has it all.

A couple of my favorite examples of how good this soundtrack is.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g3jCAyPai2Y
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_3Mo7U0XSFo

[h1][b]+Graphics[/b][/h1]
1980’s Japan never looked better as the towns of Kamurocho and Sotenbori come to life in a high resolution fashion. In-game cutscenes for Yakuza 0 are all very well done too as you’ll often be staring at the character models for long periods of time as this game’s cutscenes can go on forever so it’s always nice to make sure they look good.

[h1][b]+Minigames, minigames, and more minigames![/b][/h1]
It’s honestly quite insane just how many games within games Yakuza 0 has as you have access to so many arcade games, sports games, gambling/card games, arena fights, and special battle challenges you’ll honestly never find yourself without something to do in the game.

Personal favorites of mine are the racing minigame, blackjack, bowling, and of course Majima’s cabaret club management minigame but there’s honestly so many games to play you could easily blow a couple hours just messing around with what each town has to offer.

[h1][b]+Sidestories/Side quests[/b][/h1]
If you’re more familiar with games like Grand Theft Auto you may come to the conclusion that despite having massive open worlds, besides going on massive killing rampages and doing main story quests, there’s actually very little interesting people to meet/ things to do postgame (At least that’s been my play experience the moment i’m done with all the main quests and have nothing left to do but hunt down the last few interesting people really). 

Here though you can’t go more than two blocks before meeting an individual that may or may not be the most sane but regardless they need your help for some reason or other. These sidequests can range from a simple task, like helping a television crew film a commercial, all the way to the more wacky ones like helping a statue use the restroom or helping someone get a pizza.

Either way you'll never find yourself without something fun or wacky to do during your playtime. 

[h1][b]-Cons [/b] [/h1]

[h1][b]-Slight Issues with the PC Port[/b][/h1]
Be warned there may be a few issues regarding this PC port in particular.

During my playtime I encountered a few issues here and there, some minor some more gamebreaking.

1. Static audio ingame when talking to NPCs.

2. Inventory glitch where your entire inventory gets messed up and replaced with other ingame items.

3. Freeze into crash and since the game only lets you save at phone booths it is super painful to lose all that progress but if you get an autosave it’s not as bad but still.

[h1][b]-Minor Incovience with Kiryu’s Real-Estate Management Game[/b][/h1]
Later on you’ll unlock Kiryu’s real-estate side game where you can purchase various properties all around Kamurocho for some more cash later on than you initially invested.

The problem being that there’s really no big indicator telling you a property is available for purchase unless you actually walk up right next to it so it becomes part guessing game, part process of elimination as you walk around all the possible buildings for purchase until you find one that you can actually buy.

Edit: As others have noted if you want to have an easier time be sure to change your settings so it's much easier to find real estate properties to purchase.

[h1][b]-Very Slow Start[/b][/h1]
The first two-three hours of Yakuza 0 can be a bit of a slog to get through as you don’t have access to any of the big selling points and the game’s mechanics are slowly being released to you bit by bit.

Stick with it though as it really starts to pick up around the mid-end point stages of the game.



[h1][b]Final Verdict:(9/10)[/b] [/h1]
Yakuza 0 is an excellent open world game with too many minigames to count, lots of interesting people to meet, and of course a main storyline that’ll really put some hair on your chest with all the macho brawling. 

Overall, if you’re looking for a fun game to play with a lot of content to mess around in, considering the price of this game, you’ll definitely get your money’s worth and more.

One could yada yada endlessly about the amount of juicy content in this game, but judging from simply this it’s safe to assume this game is an absolute steal at its US$19.99 pricetag.

For reference, this is the first Yakuza game I have ever played. 

PROS:
[b]A Game of Two Halves[/b] – The games' primary strength comes from two fronts:  Its intensity and its ridiculousness. Its storyline is a fascinating one about betrayal, love, political intrigue, revenge, corruption. A lot of the cutscenes are INTENSE. Expect to see a lot of old, stern-looking Japanese men argue, shout and swear and try to kill each other. Some of the fighting scenes are brutal, with a handful having the same kind of intensity I would expect from something like Metal Gear Rising: Revengeance (the sewer tunnel and boat come to mind in particular). Some moments are very somber. Some even made me cry. This is a game that takes itself very seriously. 

Well, sometimes. See here's the thing: On the other side it is utterly silly. Expect to be prancing around singing songs in karaoke or hitting the dance floor and busting a move. Asking call girls what they're wearing so you can meet them and go out on dates. Help a pervert find his mojo. Get in a fight with a big buff bald man who wants to steal your hair? Watch softcore videos of dozens of Japanese girls. This doesn't even scratch the surface of what kind of craziness is on offer. 

It's completely insane how the game jackknifes between these two states, receive death-threats and have an attack on your life and then go and play some darts. Deal with a kidnapping then go to race tiny remote-controlled cars. It's something that makes the game very unique, very special. 

[b]The Minigames & Sidequests[/b] – And what a huge selection there are! Bowling, darts, karaoke, dancing, real estate, casino, fishing.. the list goes on and on. There's a real spectrum of entertainment on offer. Some are great fun, some aren't, but a special shoutout to the cabaret minigame which I got ADDICTED to big time. 

CONS:
[b]Endgame & Some Minigames[/b] – Found the endgame content to be pretty grindy once the main storyline had been completed and some conditions had to been met for certain sidequests. Some minigames are a pain, particularly the catfighting one which was just pure random luck and required me to break my fingers button mashing. Some minigames are very distinctly Japanese and could have done with being explained a bit better. 

CONCLUSION:
Yakuza 0 was a great game, lots of fun and I eagerly await the next installment: Yakuza Kiwami on Steam.

Yakuza Zero is an incredible title, in fact that's an understatement. I've completed the game twice already on PS4 and still find myself wanting it to play through on the PC. 

[What type of game is this?] It's a tough one this. People often compare it to GTA, but those people haven't played the game. It is not like GTA. Sometimes I hear Sleeping Dogs, no, not really, the biggest similarities is that they're both in Asia (not even the same place) In fact, there's no games like Yakuza. Above all else, it's an Action game. It has some elements of an RPG but I wouldn't call it an RPG, or even an Action RPG. It's pseudo-open world. It's a crime thriller in 80's Japan.
 
[What is it about?] You follow Kazuma Kiryu and Goro Majima as the game swaps between characters in Kamurocho and Sotenbori, two fictionalised places in Tokyo. If I told you it was about a tiny tiny plot of land (literally a few square meters) you'd probably think that's insane, but the Yakuza are after this small plot of land and set up Kiryu for murder. You spend the game trying to get to the bottom of it with twists and turns all through the game, some predictable, some not. 

The writing in the game is incredible, in fact it's probably one of the best written games I've seen. This is in my late 30's playing since pong on the Atari 2600 with thousands of games under my belt. I can only think of a few titles that can rival it. 

[But there's loads of titles! Where do I start?!] Here. Right here. This, although one of the newer games in the series, is a prelude to the franchise. It doesn't spoil anything for later titles, and it introduces you to the cast in the early eras. Having played all the Yakuza's except 3 and a couple of spin offs, this is the place to start. 

[Graphics] 7 /10 - These aren't the games selling point. They aren't terrible, and on occasion they can look down right amazing. However, some textures and the poly count is on the low end. Regardless, it does a great job at selling the locations, and the cities at night can look absolutely fantastic. Aesthetically however, the game is gorgeous, and it absolutely oozes atmosphere. 

[Sound] 7 /10 - The sound in this game is a mixed bag. Some of the crunches as you slam a jaw into the ground is incredible. However, a few sounds such as doors opening are very poor quality. It's laughable at first and you can tell it was recorded in a studio as someone stamps their feet on the ground and pushes a squeaky door to, but it actually grows on you and you start to love it. However, the Sound design is some of the games weakest points. 

[Voice] 10/10 - UNLIKE sound however, the voice acting is outstanding. If you're looking for English you're going to be out of luck, but as a Yakuza fan, you do not want this. It was tried once and it failed horribly. The voice actors are some of the best bar none. They truly sell the characters and are incredibly versatile. Even the side cast are spot on. 

[Music] 9/10 - Subjective of course, but some of the tracks are awesome. Especially when you hear a certain track, you know a special friend is appearing. Some of the darker scenes have this deep track that resonates through the headphones with an incredible oomph. 

[Story] 10/10 - This is what makes the game. If you were to buy it, and skip the cutscenes, then you'd probably not enjoy the game. It would be pointless. The writing is top notch, the acting is top notch, it's highly original (with some cliches) and it's addictive. 

[Gameplay] 8/10 - The game is incredibly fun, there is so much to love about it. However, there are a few issues which I'll touch on in a bit. It is difficult as it's really deserving of a 10/10 but I'm trying to be realistic, but the game is incredibly complicated to explain unless you play it. 

It is essentially two different games (actually, tens of different games realistically) but for the main part you play your main missions and your sub missions. The main story is incredibly dark, brutal and atmospheric. The writing is, as said, phenomenal. It's above all else serious. Then you get to the side missions, and this is where the game turns completely. They are silly, cheesy, even immature...but None of those things are a critique of the game, they can have you laughing out loud and bring a much lighter tone to the title. Whether you go on a metal gear solid stealth mission weaving around nosey old ladies to buy a kid an adult mag, or you train your domimatrix to abuse her clients correctly, all in front of childrens prying eyes the game fluently separates its stories really well. 

Then you have everything else, and there's A LOT of it. You have mini game after mini game, whether it's bowling, karaoke, darts, arcade machines (with outrun, space harrier and multiple other full titles) pocket cars, UFO catcher, twenty or so Japanese and Chinese style minigames, Rhythm based dancing, underground semi-naked girl wrestling to larger not so mini-mini games such as running an estate agent and a hostess club where you can dress up your girls and make money. There's a never ending amount of stuff to do. 
This as I've pointed out, is not an RPG but it has RPG elements. You collect your Yen, buy new abilities, weapons etc etc and there is a fair amount of grinding involved (not your typical MMO amount however, it's not that bad) but, some of the mechanics can let the gameplay down, so let's get to that

[Mechanics] - 6/10. Here lies the problem, it's a fairly new title, but still uses old Japanese style mechanics. Want to save? Run to a phonebox. Weapons break, and they break EASILY, 4-5 hits (but there's tons of them) and the game can be clunky at times. There are multiple types of cutscenes, in game, pre rendered, dialogue where they grunt and the text scrolls, or full speaking scenes. You get use to it, and this won't happen for major parts of the game but rather, the easy side missions. Healing is tedious, inventory management is poor, camera angles aren't the best and there's invisible walls. However, usually all this would instantly put me off a game, but Yakuza is so good that I almost don't want to mention these as the game is one of the best this generation, if not of all time. It's a shame but they are easily over looked. 

[Optimisation] 10/10  My PC is overkill running a 1080 TI, 8700k and 16gb 3200mhz RAM, however, it runs flawlessly, the only problem I have is you can't downsample to 5k (I have a 1440p monitor, so 4k looks bad since it's the wrong integer (1080p x4 = 4k, 1440p x4 = 5k) and while it for some reason recognises the verticle, it doesn't the horizontal, maybe this will get fixed. It does run 4k however, but I'd rather stick to 1440p on that display type. 

[Overall] - 9.5/10. Having other Yakuza's on the Ps3, this one blew me away at how insanely good it was. It has it's issues and at the start they are jarring, but you soon forget about them and get engrossed in the game. I can't tell you how many games I've played, thousands, I'd guess anywhere between 5-10k and Yakuza zero ranks among the top.
HOWEVER, it's a game you need to give a chance! The beginning is slow, and I can see people putting it down before it has even started. There is a TON of content, that will last you many, many hours, but the game doesn't start to get interesting until chapter 2, and it doesn't really open up until chapter 4. For it's price, it is a steal. You just can't go wrong. Sadly, this is a title that needs a longer 2 hour refund window because as I said, it just doesn't open up right away. This is however, one of the best games to come out in it's year (in a year that had so many great titles, Persona 5, HZ:D etc) and it's incredible that Sega brought it to PC. It's genre is so broad and can appeal to so many people without them knowing, I highly suggest picking it up, be aware of some annoying mechanics before you go into it, and have a blast...and DO NOT SKIP THE CUTSCENES.

Yakuza 0 is a third person action game focusing on melee combat, which is set in Tokyo and Osaka in the 1980s. This is the first time I’ve played a Yakuza game. The franchise contains multiple games on Playstation, but this is the first one that has come to PC. I’m pleased that it did, because I’ve really enjoyed playing it.

The story is excellent, very well written and featuring many interesting characters. Several families within the Yakuza are fighting over control of a piece of land which is key to an extremely valuable real estate deal. It has a fascinating combination of the criminal underworld, mixed with the Japanese sense of honour. As the story progresses, the player will switch between controlling two characters, Kiryu and Majima, who both get caught up in the conflict. Cutscenes have a very cinematic feel due to the way the camera pans and zooms during conversations. There’s also fantastic detail in characters’ faces and clothing designs. Voice acting is Japanese, with subtitles.

Both cities feel alive, with lots of civilians wandering around, and gangs that will attack you on sight. You can eat food to regain health at restaurants, and you’ll encounter lots of side quests with wacky characters. For example there’s a young child who queued up for hours to buy the last copy of a new video game, only to have it stolen by an older kid. And there’s a guy doing performance art on a bridge where he’s pretending to be a statue, he desperately needs a bathroom break, but he doesn’t want anybody to see him move.

You can also entertain yourself with a wide variety of minigames. You can play pool and darts in a bar, visit a casino to play roulette, blackjack and poker, play classic Sega games Outrun and Space Harrier in an arcade, visit a bowling alley, perform karaoke, dancing, and several other activities. Some of these minigames are let down by poor control schemes, but even if you only enjoy playing a couple of these games, you could easily get a few hours entertainment.

Later in the story you’ll gain ownership of a real estate company and a nightclub. You’ll need to compete with rival businesses to gain massive profits and then spend the cash on levelling up your combat skills.

Combat is a mixed bag, not as good as the likes of Batman Arkham or Shadow of Mordor, but I’ve also played worse. After I’d levelled Majima up a bit and unlocked some special moves, I started to enjoy his slugger fighting style, where he uses a baseball bat to quickly deal with large groups of enemies. But I didn’t always enjoy Kiryu’s combat. I focused on his rush style which was okay at first, but later in the game against bosses or large crowds I felt a bit weak. Maybe his other fighting styles are better (or I just don’t fully understand how to play rush), but I didn’t want to spend hours earning enough cash to level up another style.

It took me around 39 hours to finish the story and a bunch of side quests, but there’s still plenty of stuff I haven’t done yet, which means value for money is great at the full price. I didn’t suffer from any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate. The game told me that real Yakuza use a gamepad, so I played with my X360 pad, which worked fine.

Yakuza 0 is a mostly enjoyable game which you should consider picking up. And I hope Sega will bring more of these games to PC.

[h1] Playing all Yakuza/Like a Dragon games in 2024 (1/12) [/h1]

[b] Yakuza 0 [/b]

I bought this game a couple of years ago and never played it beyond the first hour, but as the release of the new "Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth" approached I wanted to try playing this one, go to Like a Dragon and then play the new one.

It was a serious mistake, what seemed like a simple plan turned into a research project about the saga, about what games to play, in what order to play them, what spin offs to play and also learning a lot about Japanese culture.

And speaking on that topic, I have never been much of a "fan" of Japan, not that I have anything against the country and its culture, but I have never been interested in them, but there is one thing that makes me fall in love with the country, and It is [b]SUSHI[/b], and I think that Sushi is, for me, the best way to describe what this game is.

I heard a lot about sushi, about how tasty it is, about how great it is and many other things, but I never dared to try it, mainly due to ignorance, there are a lot of different types of sushi, a lot of names unknown to me, and a lot of ingredients that I had never heard of, just like there are a large number of games in the Yakuza series, with different names and it is even difficult to know in what order they go.

Both the game and the sushi are designed by people who live in a completely different culture than mine and who see and feel the world in a completely different way. But in the end, it just fits, all those flavors that you've never tried, that don't taste like anything you've ever eaten before, they just fit.

This game is simply incredible for a lot of different reasons, but I want to mainly highlight a few points:

[b]The world[/b] is one of the main protagonists of the story, it is incredible how it feels so alive and so real despite the years, something that I can believe exists, with a lot of things to do, it just makes me want to take a walk for hours. After finishing the game I spent hours watching videos about Japan and Tokyo, learning about the experiences of people who have visited the country and making me understand more about the country, creating in me an interest that I had never had about the country.

And no, I'm not in love with the country, and to be completely honest, it doesn't seem like a country I would ever want to live in (although I would really like to visit it sometime), but it really makes you see that the world as you see it is not the same for everyone, and that's pretty cool.

[b]The Story[/b] is also one of the strong points of the game, with super interesting characters and although I have always had difficulty remembering names and faces in video games, and names in different languages ​​are even more difficult, I can clearly remember almost all the characters important parts of this game.

The [b]voice acting[/b] is top-notch, I never thought, seeing how "silly" this game was before I started playing it, that I would be able to get so excited and attached to characters because of the way they are interpreted, even though I don't understand a single word of the VO, there are cinematics and stories that are simply, in my opinion, [b]some of the best you can find in this industry.[/b]

And mainly, the game is just [b]fun[/b], the story is fun, the secondary parts are often even funnier, and generally, the gameplay is pretty fun too. The main ways to get money and some of the minigames could be a smooth standalone game, where you can spend a lot of hours without getting tired of them.

Although I must say that the combat, which is good, begins to lose its charm a little over the hours, I think the number of combats is a little abused, and I could win a little if I had a little less of them (I write this after having played a couple more games and I must say that, unfortunately, this game is much better in that sense than some that follow)

But overall, it's an incredible game, quite unique, that made me go from being a little curious to buying just over 10 games after finishing this one. I really recommend it.

[b]95/100[/b]

[h1] Yakuza 0: Is it just a Japanese GTA? [/h1]

[i] Yakuza 0 [/i] is the first Yakuza release for PC as well as a great start for the PC releases, as it is a prequel for the whole series. Set in fictional district of Kamurocho, Tokyo and Sotenbori, Osaka, the player takes control of two characters, Kiryu and Majima. With these two yakuza (ex)members, players embark on ridiculous, epic and tragic adventures which will leave many players scratching their heads, asking what the hell just happened. Many people said that it is just a japanese GTA but let's dive into Yakuza underworld and decide ourselves how much truth that is. 

[b] Gameplay - 8/10 [/b]

Let's get one thing of the table right away. [i] Yakuza 0 [/i] is nothing like GTA. If I would have to make a comparison, it is closer to [i] Sleeping Dogs [/i] but even that is not quite right. Same as [i] Sleeping Dogs [/i], Yakuza relies heavily on melee combat, however that is taken even more into depth. The depth comes in with three distinctive fighting styles for both Kiryu and Majima. For Kiryu, we have the balanced Brawler; focusing on hitting as hard as possible, while having decent mobility as well as defense, quick and light Rush; with it's fast dodge for circling your enemies and light attacks which can stun the enemy and finally brutal and ruthless Beast; which uses objects around the character to attack multiple enemies at once with high damage, sacrificing speed and mobility..

Majima on the other hand, has the dirty and underhanded Thug; almost the same as Kiryu's Brawler, except focused more moving around the enemy and using the right moment to strike, breakdancing (yes you read that correctly) Breaker; which uses breakdancing moves to attack everyone around you while being highspeed, and baseball bat wielding Slugger; who has very high single target damage and block which can counter most of the enemy attacks. Each of this fighting styles has its own skill tree, where you can upgrade them using money you gain as you play. As you can see, Yakuza does take its pride in its combat, which is enhanced by weapons that can be gathered and received throughout the game.
 
Concerning gameplay, we are just still on the top of the iceberg. Outside of the main storyline, players have several other longer quest plotlines to explore, such as running a real estate empire or running a cabaret club (I did spend way too much time dressing up girls). Am I hearing voices saying that it is still not enough? You have cca 50 different sidequests that you can pursue, each more ridiculous than the previous one. And if that is still not enough foir you, there is a bunch of Sega classic arcade games as minigames as well as other outlets for your needs such as karakoe, disco, mahjong, shogi, baseball, bowling and watching erotic videos (I swear I did it for the achievement). 

However, as you progress through the game, you will get more and more annoyed by random enemy encounters which will be just plain boriing and repetetive as you continue to upgrade your fighting abilites. Moreover, there are few immersion breaking setpieces when you take into consideration that Kiryu claims he would never kill a person (car chase, I am looking at you).

[b] Story - 10/10 [/b]

The story in this game is phenomenal. It all starts with Kiryu being framed for a murder but devolves into a much bigger thing than anyone could ever anticipate. Suddenly, you are not only trying to clear your own name but also trying to fight off the entire yakuza clan.  And almost on the other side of Japan, a seemingly irrelevant story of Majima begins with one of the fanciest combat tutorials ever. I cannot possibly say how these two stories connect without spoiling the entire game. But I can for sure say that this story is filled with action, sadness, mystery and epic fights to the brim and there won't be a single moment when you will be bored. [i] Yakuza 0 [/i] is not fighting two tigers barehanded insane, but it is still pretty insane and great and after you finish it, you will gladly jump into Kiwami.

[b] Characters - 8/10 [/b]

There is a thing every good writer knows. Characters make the story and story makes the characters. [i] Yakuza 0 [/i] is the perfect example of that. From charismatic, emphatetic yet ruthless Kiryu to absolutely insane Majima, every major character gets properly developed and you don't feel like they are there without any reason. Except for the main villain, who almost does not make sense to be the main villain for the Kiryu story, as you do not seem his nearly enough for you to form any kind of feelings towards him. However, outside of that one major hiccup, every other character will grow in some way in your heart, no matter if you hate or love them.

[b] Visuals - 8/10 [/b]

[i] Yakuza 0 [/i] looks good, however it could be better and more senseful. You have several types of cutscenes which can sometimes be immersion ruining. First of the group is normal regular fullscreen cutscene, which can luckily be uncapped from 30FPS to 60FPS. Second type is where it is using gameplay visuals with visual novel styled text boxes. The third and the last style is still images with bigger text boxes on the side of the screen. There would also be no issue whatsoever, however not only are these cutscenes placed sometimes in weird moments but also the third type is used maybe 3 times in the whole game. It almost feels like it is unnecessary for it to be there. And that is the biggest issue with how the game looks, the unnatural cutscenes and framing of important story elements. 

[b] Sound and Music - 10/10 [/b]

First things first, music in [i] Yakuza 0 [/i] is absolutely phenomenal. Not only you have different music for bossfights, depending on who the boss is but you also have different theme song for each of the fighting styles, making you sometimes choose a style just based on the fact you like that song. Second aspect is the voice acting, which might be an issue for some players. There is no English dubbing, only Japanese with English subtitles. However, the voice acting is amazing, it feels real and you can almost hear the love everyone put into their respective voiced characters. You will understand what I mean once you hear Majima going absolutely mad. 

[b] Should I get this game? [/b]

It would be unfair of me to just YES immidiately, so let me ask you 3 simple questions:
1. Are you looking for a masterfully written story from a criminal underworld?
2. Do you enjoy fighting games with fresh take on the genre?
3. Are you looking for hours upon hours of endless fun?

If you answered YES to any of these questions, go break some jaws in Yakuza aniki!

[b] PC Specifications for reference [/b]

Graphics card: GeForce 940M 2GB
Memory: 8GB RAM [/quote]

Yakuza. Japanese open-world game about Japan, its organized crime, and the world around. Many strong characters, tons of very specific, dramatically oversized situations and reactions, based on the Japanese culture. Thousands of fights, with many different fighting styles applied, plus some shootouts and other vivid action.

Some people say that Yakuza is like GTA... but different. Like Shenmue, only better. And many people familiar with the whole Yakuza series crowns Yakuza Zero as the best in the whole line. At least, the best one for newcomers, with the best story-telling and many diverse activities to prolong the gameplay and satisfy the player. And oh boy. That's the truth. But not the whole truth.

You see, the main game progress is based on the street brawls (aka 'beat'em up'). You'll not get anywhere far if you don't enjoy that part. But... most of the fights are happening when you just stroll the streets, going from one mission location to another, or just looking for someone in need of help (=sidequests). A typical deal for the Japanese (not exclusively) games since the '80s: you walk your way, mind your own business, but every 10 meters you walk, there'll be some gangbangers waiting for you. And get me right, the fights are really fun in Yakuza! For some time. But most of the typical goons are not giving you any challenge, except for being the targets. No strategy, no brain is applied. Of course, you can get creative. One of the best Yakuza features is the level of backstage interactivity. You are free to use in your fights thousands of items you see on the street: parked bikes, trashcans, advertising stands, benches - and many more! Plus, some of the combos and combo-moves involving the different environments, are really a must-see! But... even that level of freedom to bash around wears off after some time.

The game is so full of various activities, quests, collectible items - if you really want to get perfect from this game, you'll need probably 200+ hours, but even if you're not a 'completionist', and just look for the story, you still be involved into very lengthy mini-games, which are unlocking story progress events. So, even if you are trying to avoid the most part of the supplementary stuff, which this game is so proud of, you still bound to spend about 30-40+ hours just going through the story. And... the freshness of combat in the game wears much, much faster. IF there were not that many brainless goons on every corner, I wouldn't probably felt the weariness about Yakuza. At least, not that soon. It took more than a month for me to beat the game - not because it's too hard, but because of that mind-boiling combination of too many too generic fights, too many strange and time-consuming mini-games (starting with karaoke and dancing) PLUS that famous for Japanese games Overreacting and Drama. All of those are unskippable, for the most part.

So. To summarize. A great story, really recommended. It's the story part that makes Yakuza better than Shenmue and GTA. As of the fights, the battle system... Let's say it's fun, for a time. But is it better than in Shenmue? NO! Despite all the interactivity, all the battle styles, charismatic masters teaching your characters really nice moves in the best way possible - the hard way - it is still just a 2-3 button mish-mash, for the most part of gameplay. Not really THAT engaging, as it was in Shenmue, where you really had to think about your moves, distances, timings, and stuff. So, I really disagree with those who say that fighting in Yakuza is better than in Shenmue. Less clunky, due to the better controls layout - yes, obviously. Easier (even on the Legend difficulty without buffs), bizarre, defiant - but not better. As for 100% completion and mini-games... I don't mind dancing, karaoke, darts... But RNG dating sim! Even more RNG-based cat fights! And neverending punks on every corner! Wiped out my passion to play it more. Still, a 9/10 mark. Cool game.

The two main characters go through absolute hell, routinely do and see things which, if they happened to you, would most likely make you stare at the ceiling in irreversible catatonic shock until you shrivelled up and died; yet here they are, fifteen minutes later, partying like there's no tomorrow in a karaoke bar, racing pocket circuit cars with seven-year-olds or [b][url=https://i.redd.it/6nadkgfku2171.jpg]choosing the best hair accessory for the prettiest hostess.[/url][/b] 

And it works.

[h2] What this review is not [/h2]
🈁 As much as I would like it to be the case, this review is by no means a comprehensive analysis of Yakuza 0. Writing one in 8000 characters would simply be impossible – the game is [b]TOO BIG.[/b] There is so much stuff to do, so many side activities, so many things to talk about that I'd easily exhaust the character limit yet barely scratch the surface of why the game is so bloody awesome. 

Here's a tip – let this review be your [i]last[/i] one. Screw it – go in blind, let this prequel to a great franchise sweep you off your feet. I will, however, outline just a couple of things I want you to be aware of before you start. Don't worry though, it will literally be a couple, as in "two".

[h3] Cutscenes... are super long [/h3]
🈴 I mean, [b][url=https://i.redd.it/qmd6r2arebm61.jpg]super-duper freaking long.[/url][/b] The first bunch of cutscenes that introduce one of the main characters is a whopping 9 minutes and 33 seconds long – yes, I timed it. Most games would have you at level 5 by that point; if you're the kind to rush and look for an actual [u][i]game[/i][/u] to [u][i]play[/i][/u], you might wanna hold this one off for a while. The second character's introduction is TWICE as long, by the way – only to be twice as amazing.

You see, Yakuza 0 is not afraid of being a movie. It's got 4 types of cutscenes that it uses to great effect; a story of this scale and magnitude would be impossible to tell otherwise. I'll tell you what, maybe take a risk – even if you think you're not a cutscene guy or gal, this masterpiece of a game might just be the thing to change your mind. 

My girlfriend, who was unimpressed at first, was glued to the screen till the very end when she saw what Majima and Kiryu were going through. The cinematic nature of the game makes it perfect for backseating.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2634308775
[h3] Completionist heaven... or hell? [/h3]
🈯 I swear to god I'm not making this up – Yakuza 0 has a thing called Completion List that you see when you press pause. It's a list of all the things you can do in the game, separated into 5 different categories: Adventure, Battle, Business, Substories and Minigames. Where else have you seen that, huh? 

Each time you fulfil a specific requirement, you get a pleasant notification and are awarded with a Completion Point (CP). If you have enough of them, you may purchase different upgrades to make your time spent in the game considerably easier and more fun. Developers [u]encourage[/u] completion, and it's a big part of enjoying the game for many people; it took me 175 hours to complete everything Yakuza 0 had to offer, and it was [i]mostly[/i] time well spent. I say mostly because, unfortunately, [b][url=https://i.redd.it/hhkawwv7doi71.jpg]there's a hitch[/url][/b] – some of the challenges are downright insane.

😫 Are you willing to learn mahjong? Because you're gonna have to learn mahjong, which is, like, one of the most complex strategy games ever – possibly the most complex out there. Be ready to spend at least 10 hours trying to get 6 CPs associated with it. Oh, and it's also in every next Yakuza game after 0. Buckle up! You're in for a ride.

😫 Are you willing to go up against a boss who can combo you into oblivion and take 3/4 of your health in five seconds while you can barely land a single hit? And he has [u]five[/u] (!) health bars. This is one of the notorious Climax Battles – ridiculously difficult challenges specifically designed to make you fly off the handle.

😫 Are you willing to participate in so-called "catfights"? When I first heard of them at the beginning of the game, I didn't know I'd be seeing much less fur and much more bare oily skin of scantily-clad ladies duking it out in a wrestling ring. You bet on a winner and RNGeesus decides your fate – except that the game's rigged and you'll most likely lose. 

I could go on, but you get the gist. You'll need to work hard to get all achievements, so I hope you enjoy the process as much as I do, otherwise don't even attempt it – save yourself some agony and frustration. The feeling of pure joy when you complete everything, however, is too big to put into words.

[h2] Conclusion(s) [/h2]
✔️ Great game – open your wallets, people!
🛑 Action addicts and completionists – beware!

🈳 Congratulations – you have somehow reached the end of this review! You must truly be a dedicated person if you've made it all the way down here through my incoherent ramblings. I have nothing else to say that could be even remotely worthwhile, so I'll stop wasting your time, like, right now.

Yakuza 0 accomplished two things: it got me very interested in the Yakuza series as a whole and it earned a spot in my must-play recommendation list. I recommend it as reflexively as I recommend established classics like DOOM and Age of Empires. It isn't perfect, but it does so many things so well that I'd be doing the world a disservice by not recommending it.

Steam says I have 120-ish hours, but in reality I only spent about 90-ish, maybe just short of 100 hours. It was all time well spent and I wouldn't trade it for any other game.

Yakuza 0 does something really well that a lot of "open world" games just aren't good at doing: making you want to actually explore the world and do all the little minigames and experience all the sidestories within it. The only game that's ever done that for me was STALKER. I'm not going to lie, I disliked a bunch of the minigames: I didn't like dancing that much, I was bad at pool, the two catfights I gambled on were a waste of time, and I'm not about to learn mahjong or shogi for some completion points and yen.

However, just going around Kamurocho and Sotenbori and fighting with all the wild abilities and heat actions, running the financial mechanics, eating at all the food joints and going "man that looks tasty, I think I need to actually go over there in real life one of these days", helping people around town, using all the weapons you end up collecting along the way? [b]THAT[/b] is what video gaming is all about. Not to mention that the story is genuinely interesting and has plenty of twists and turns to bring you into the series excited to find out what comes next.

For every annoyance that I ran into playing Yakuza 0, there was a litany of other enjoyable gameplay moments that overwrote the annoyance. Again, Yakuza 0 is a game that you need to play to at least form an opinion on. I guarantee you'll like [b][i]something[/i][/b] about it.

RGG Studio's magnum opus. People tell you to play this game first if you want to get into Yakuza. With the recent release of the money-grabbing "Director's Cut" and the even more despicable Kiwami 3, Yakuza is looking like its run its course, at long last. If I recall correctly, this version of the game has been taken off the steam store, and you can only see the Director's Cut now, so nobody looking to buy 0 can even see this review. That's okay. This is more of a love letter anyway.

I love this game. I think it's really something special, even outside of the context of the greater Yakuza franchise. Since it chronologically comes first, anybody can play it and enjoy it- this was how I first experienced the game before playing Kiwami 1 and 2. I will get around to 3, 4, 5 and 6 one day, but I'm still on the fence about the 'Like a Dragon' games, because to me, they signify the beginning of the end. Either way, Yakuza 0 is pretty magical, at least to me. It's hard to describe in an objective way. This game really makes you care about the characters- even ones you don't traditionally like, or think are good people. I teared up at least twice, maybe more. They're endearing, funny, complex, and saddening, of course. I will always mourn Lord of the Night Majima because I think he is easily the best version of the character, and a protagonist I love even more than Kiryu.

The soundtrack is superb. Of course, a lot of tracks are remixes, or include leitmotifs from older Yakuza songs, but that just goes to show that if this series has one consistent property, it's that the music is stellar. T u s k, Reign, the English intro theme, Pledge of Demon and Mad Dog Unleashed (unfortunately unreleased) are my personal favourites.

Story. Even though 0 is the BEST of the Yakuza games, it's still a Yakuza game, and the story can be convoluted, all over the place, and a little confusing at times. However, this doesn't detract from the emotional storytelling and overall impact of the story. It's great, superb- just a little hard to wrap your head around sometimes. Much easier on a repeat playthrough. Or maybe I'm just a little dumb.

With almost 60 hours in the game at the time of writing this review (and probably more later), I'm still finding myself barely breaching the surface of the combat system of this game. It probably doesn't help that I'm on K&M unlike a real yakuza. You can passably beat this game mashing buttons with minimal thought, but that isn't fun and ends up being more frustrating than anything. Of course, that's not how the game was meant to be played. Learn combos. Make your own movesets. It's very satisfying to chain attacks together that you've learned and know will be effective against your enemy. But like I said, I'm still a total noob when it comes to fighting in this game. Also, throw bicycles at people.

So, do I recommend this game? Absolutely. It's great. I love it. You'll love it too. I think this is one of those games that comes around only a few times in your life that leaves a little notch in your heart where it'll stay forever, not just a game you play, enjoy, and leave behind. Even if it takes years, this is one of those games you'll come back to. 9/10.

Yakuza 0 is a wonderful addition to the Yakuza series. The strong story and the many, often humorous, mini-games provide many hours of fun.
An attractive slip-on in the form of Yakuza 0.
This game takes place where it all begins, which is the great 80s.
Yakuza 0 is therefore a prequel which is an excellent choice for the first Yakuza.

The game also works great on a steam deck: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TRD5ppWpW7c

Since this game is about the Japanese mafia, fighting cannot be missed.
From drunken strangers to tattooed Yakuza bosses, almost no one escapes Kiryu and Majima's fists.
In the beginning you can get away with blindly approaching a brawl, but the final bosses in particular require some form of strategy.
During the game you have the opportunity to develop your character. This means that you can buy new moves that you can use in battles.
The fighting is quite repetitive, but nevertheless never really gets boring. The opponents are always different and that, together with the use of new moves, ensures that it remains fun.

Yakuza Zero is also a great game graphically. The character models of the main characters in the story look good, and the animations are also smooth. Unfortunately, this does not always apply to the NPCs in the area, but we just add this to the humorous part of the game.
Fortunately, it is not disturbing anywhere, since it belongs to the genre a bit. The world of Yakuza doesn't seem huge at first glance either, but the moment you start playing you realize that the world out there is crammed with details and ways to pass your time.
So in this case there is clearly a focus on quality of the world over quantity.

Yakuza 0 is not only a perfect entry point for new people, it is also the best game in the series.
Thanks to a wonderful 80s vibe, a sharp story and improved gameplay, the series is at its peak.
Yakuza 0 thus transcends the classification of 'simple prequel' and is elevated to an essential game.
